I love this game so much. Haven't tried solo yet, but couch co-op was great! Wish there was an upgrade for my husband's multitasking skills though. Update: I have now played solo and am a full blown addict. Husband is concerned. The discord community for this game is really nice too - people are very friendly and willing to answer questions. The founders/devs are also active and regularly check for feedback and active bugs. However, the level of skill from some of the players and being able to always see a live leaderboard in the game has TRULY humbled me.
Less than 6 months after release dev has stopped support to work on a new game instead of fixing existing game. I would not support the dev as they do not support their players.

My only gripe is that every game can feel endless. Would like to be able to complete or opt out after a certain amount of days. Spent about 3.5 hours in one game which was a blast, but was exhausting and can't really commit that much time every time i want to play the game. Otherwise we just never return to a game nor want to kill ourselves to start over. Will recommend the game once there's a way to "win" a game Another game played for about 3 hours with two friends and unfortunately lost connection. I couldn't join back in and we lost before being able to unlock the next weaponry. The game itself is fun and has a lot of great mechanics. The only issue is the online co-op is unplayable as it is extremely laggy. I'd estimate a consistent 500ms-1000ms delay. It was really good in remote play with very little delay which unfortunately increased my play time and I was unable to refund the game. I do want to support the developers, but my copy was purchased to be able to play the online co-op which I was not able to do. If the online co-op is fixed, then I would recommend the game for others that seek to play online with friends. If it's an issue on my end, please let me know what I can do to fix.

I went in really wanting to love this, but it feels like an early access with too many poor design choices holding it back. I really hope these issues are addressed. Gameplay Issues - The small doors on the sides are nearly impossible to see without muscle memory. My girlfriend spent half the time trying to exit or enter the crafting room. Just make them holes in the fence instead of small doors that can't be seen from above. - Blowing up 4 gems is mentioned as a tip but ONLY possible with pixel perfect accuracy. Why? Why not make them spawn in groups of 4 so it's not needlessly tedious. - Smart loaders rip items out of their spot before they're even ready. I lost a round because my smart loader was taking the cannonballs out of the water before they cooled off, leading to a huge backup of red-hot cannonballs and burned irons, while being unable to actually do anything. - Carrying 1 gem at a time just feels bad, considering they're always placed as far away as possible. Visuals - The game is way too dark/vibrant at night, making it hard on the eyes. - Could not get the camera to zoom in, in coop, making it very difficult to see anything. I found out later after my GF already quit that B toggles camera in singleplayer. Unsure if this works in Coop, but why does coop default to zoomed out? Can it even be toggled there? - The IMPACT style font should be reserved for titles only, it's very hard to read screens full of it. - Some text is misleading.. DoubleCannons says it holds 2 cannonballs. Does it fire both out at once? Or does 1 cannonball fire 2 shots? (so 4 total) Overall, good potential, just not worth the $20 as it's just not up to the quality or content of many games like it.

[h3]Industrious chaos and factory fun ensues as a bunch of animals defend their forge from ferocious foes Plants vs Zombies style..[/h3] FIrst and foremost, I really enjoy the Overcooked kind of games where a bunch of deranged individuals are unleashed on an already cramped space trying to fulfill tasks while tripping over each other's tails.. In Keep Keepers you are cooking with gas, but instead of cakes you are serving bombs to witless invaders of your forgeworld! Each round consists of a series of ways of enemies encroaching on your turf, and it is up to you and your cohort to drive them back. To defend against the invader you need to build bombs, mortar shells and other high caliber ammunition to your everhungering defensive artillery. The marriage of this industrial mayhem with a palatable modular tower defense game that reminds me of the old classic Plants vs Zombies is a rather simple yet genial thing. Keep Keepers captures this sense of foreboding chaos really well while simultaneously presenting a smooth joyful coop experience where automation really serves as your battleplans beating heart. Now, first and foremost, this is a multiplayer co-op game at heart and deserves to be treated as such. I did try to play this solo for a while, and take my word for it, it was not an enjoyable experience.. However, if you do happen to have a bunch of stress tolerant mechanicum-aligned friends, this is a hidden gem in the automation/management/tower defense genre that really works marvels in combining the chaos on the factory floor with a deeper sense of strategic planning that always tend to break in the most deranged of situations. The devs have been releasing updates generously during my time with the game, and although there are some optimisation issues they are minor and do not get in the way of the beating heart of the gameplay experience. All in all this is a fun and quirky base defense kind of game that truly deserves more love and is a hearty recommendation in the jolly couch co-op category!. This game is a Diamond in the rough. Absolutely hands down amazing. The thought and care that went into this game is top tier. It combines tower defence with resource management and automation, all categories I love. Truly though it's about how they combined them into one seamless game that makes you think well still being enjoyable. Going into this game it looked fun but me and my Friend had our concerns about how well it would play and how much depth it would have. However it blew us both out of the water that it's mechanics are straightforward and simple but allow for high end complexity well having tons of content to explore. This is a game I feel I will be able to come back to time and time again over the years and enjoy over and over.

The game has a really solid foundation. I found myself immediately thinking of the potential automation and offense options that await me. Where it falls flat is in small, but numerous ways. While I think the idea of having to weigh the value in upgrading shop slots to get access to better automation items is cool, it leaves too much to chance. In PlateUp (the clear inspiration for this game), you can utilize the Research Bench, Copy Machine, and Blueprint Cabinets to gain more control over your tools. If you get a basic stove in the store, you can use the Research bench to upgrade that into a safety hob. In Keep Keepers, if you're looking for the safety furnace, you have ZERO control or other options than praying it appears in your store via rerolling. That lack of control leads to runs feeling entirely RNG dependent. As far as weaponry goes, the game could use some variety. In the basic mode, you start with a basic cannon. You can find a double cannon or buzzsaw in your store, or you can upgrade either of your cannon types with elemental ammunition. That is the extent of it. Once you have your desired element, beyond a couple of small buffs from the totems, you cannot improve your offense capabilities. The entire fun of tower defense games is constantly upgrading and improving your towers until you are obliterating the massive waves of enemies with your supreme defenses. Keep Keepers fails to achieve this in any meaningful way, leading to no real motivation to push to higher waves. Automation of ammunition and econ combined with tower defense elements sounds amazing on paper and even feels good at the start. Unfortunately, the game fails to follow through on making these elements rewarding, causing the waves to feel like chores rather than be enjoyable to watch your chaotic cannon factory consume the enemy forces. What pains me the most is these issues can easily be solved through the addition of a few new tools akin to the PlateUp Research Bench variations and upgradable defenses. Apparently, the dev has foregone any future development on the game for financial concerns, which while valid, mean the game will remain in the mediocre and uninspired state I found it to be.

Hidden gem (literally :). My sister and I are always looking for new co-op games. This one far exceeded our expectations! It is a seamless blend of base management/automation and tower defense. Plus, you get to run around as cute animals.
It's like overcooked but more junk and more chill. Had a good time for a few evenings with friends. Not too challenging, which is good for me.

Tower defense mixed with PlateUp! sounds like a perfect combo. It’s the kind of game I thought about before realizing it already existed. Unfortunately, I just couldn’t enjoy it. I really tried, but the gameplay kept frustrating me despite how polished everything is. I think it might work better with a few changes: cannons auto-firing, less rigid lane defense, or a different approach to the elemental system. The side-to-side movement and returning gems also felt more tedious than fun. In summary, the game plays tight and is polished, but they'd need to change very thing about the game to make it fun.

Keep Keepers, developed and published by Thunderrock Innovations, takes a familiar collection of genres and combines them into a fast-paced cooperative experience that thrives on teamwork and adaptability. At its core, the game is a roguelite tower defense title where players are entrusted with protecting a magical keep from increasingly dangerous waves of enemies. However, the game goes beyond simply placing defenses and waiting for attacks to unfold. It introduces resource gathering, base expansion, and automation systems that constantly demand the player's attention, creating a gameplay loop that feels energetic from beginning to end. The title's biggest selling point is its emphasis on cooperative play. Whether playing locally or online, players are encouraged to divide tasks and communicate efficiently. One person may focus on harvesting resources while another upgrades defensive structures or repairs damaged sections of the keep. As enemy assaults intensify, these responsibilities become more demanding, forcing teams to make quick decisions under pressure. This constant need for coordination gives Keep Keepers an almost party-game atmosphere despite its strategic foundation. Victories feel earned because they are often the result of effective planning and split-second problem-solving. Progression is another area where the game performs well. Each run provides opportunities to unlock new improvements and refine strategies, giving players a reason to return after every defeat. The roguelite framework ensures that failure is part of the experience rather than a punishment. Players gradually discover more efficient ways to build their fortress, optimize their economy, and automate repetitive tasks. Watching a modest settlement evolve into a heavily fortified stronghold is one of the game's most satisfying aspects, and the sense of advancement remains rewarding throughout multiple sessions. From a presentation standpoint, Keep Keepers opts for a charming and accessible visual style. Its colorful environments and readable interface make it easy to keep track of the action, even when the screen becomes crowded with enemies and effects. Character and creature designs fit comfortably within the fantasy setting, while the soundtrack and sound effects do a good job of reinforcing the urgency of battle. Although the game does not aim for graphical realism, its artistic direction complements the gameplay and ensures that clarity is never sacrificed for spectacle. There are, however, a few limitations worth mentioning. Players seeking a purely single-player experience may find that some of the excitement diminishes without companions sharing the workload. Additionally, while the roguelite systems add replay value, the overall gameplay loop can become somewhat repetitive during extended play sessions. Certain strategies eventually emerge as more reliable than others, which may reduce experimentation for veteran players. Fortunately, the game's cooperative focus and procedural elements do enough to keep most sessions feeling fresh. Keep Keepers succeeds because it understands the appeal of cooperative chaos. By combining tower defense mechanics with roguelite progression, resource management, and automation, Thunderrock Innovations has created a title that is easy to pick up yet challenging to master. It may not revolutionize the genre, but it delivers a polished and entertaining experience that rewards teamwork and strategic thinking. For players looking for a multiplayer game that balances accessibility with depth, Keep Keepers is a worthwhile addition to their library. Rating: 8/10
